slides.title: Hilbert's Axioms as a Working Geometry
slides.notes: Open by framing Hilbert's project as a repair of hidden assumptions rather than a rejection of Euclid. The source span covers printed pages 65 through 116, and the notebook turns those ideas into inspectable model properties. The central habit for the lecture is to ask what permission a proof step is using, and whether a proposed model actually supplies it.

slides.title: Five Axial Questions
slides.notes: Use this route as a contract with the audience. The chapter has many named axioms, but the cognitive load drops if each group answers one question about geometric action. Emphasize that the later slides will repeatedly compare good behavior in the real plane with failures in rational or finite models.

slides.title: Undefined Terms, Defined Behavior
slides.notes: Stress the difference between a drawing and a model. A drawing suggests relations, while the axioms specify which relations are legal and how they interact. This is the first shift from Euclidean practice to Hilbert's formal method: proofs become portable because they no longer depend on visual assumptions that were never stated.

slides.title: Two Points Should Select One Line
slides.notes: This slide uses a finite affine model as a microscope for incidence, not as a full Hilbert plane. The highlighted row line is only one of the carriers; the important fact is that all unordered pairs behave the same way. Mention that the notebook checks this by counting line memberships rather than trusting the visual grid.

slides.title: Existence Is Not Enough: Uniqueness Can Fail
slides.notes: Now make the failure concrete. If two different carriers both pass through the same pair of points, a later argument cannot refer to the unique line determined by those points. The drawing is intentionally simple because the mathematical warning is about language: without uniqueness, many familiar proof steps stop being functions.

slides.title: Betweenness Turns Lines Into Ordered Places
slides.notes: Betweenness is the first place where the picture of a line gains an internal order. The relation is not just a convenience for drawing segments; it is the device that makes rays, interiors, and crossing arguments meaningful. Ask students to notice how much ordinary Euclidean language quietly assumes this order has already been installed.

slides.title: Pasch Is the Warning Light for Hidden Order
slides.notes: Pasch is easy to underestimate because the real-plane drawing feels self-evident. In Hilbert's framework the point is exactly that such separation behavior deserves an axiom. Connect this to the notebook's sign-change test: the computation gives a modern way to see what the order axiom is protecting.

slides.title: Segment Congruence Is a Transport Tool
slides.notes: Keep the word transport in the foreground. Segment congruence is not merely saying two lengths compare; it gives a construction-like permission to place a copy on a chosen ray. This is the bridge from Euclid's hands-on operations to Hilbert's relational language.

slides.title: Angle Copying Plus SAS Powers Triangle Proofs
slides.notes: Present SAS as an axiom with computational personality: it is a constraint propagation rule. Once the included angle and adjacent sides are matched, the rest of the triangle data cannot drift independently. The notebook's residual check models this idea by applying a rigid motion and verifying that the forced quantities agree up to numerical precision.

slides.title: A Neutral Plane Is Already Rich
slides.notes: This is the pause point where students often realize that neutral geometry is not empty geometry. Incidence, order, and congruence already support a substantial body of arguments. The important separation is that parallel behavior and certain intersection existence results are not smuggled into the definition of a Hilbert plane.

slides.title: Different Models Fail Different Switches
slides.notes: Use the matrix diagnostically rather than taxonomically. The real coordinate plane is the standard friendly model, but the rational plane and finite affine plane expose why the axiom groups are separate. Students should leave this slide with the habit of asking for a witness of failure, not merely labeling a model as familiar or unfamiliar.

slides.title: The Rational Plane Looks Euclidean Until It Does Not
slides.notes: The rational plane is a good stress test because it preserves many algebraic-looking habits while failing at existence. The circles in the visual would intersect in the real plane, but their intersection coordinates leave the rational field. This is why the chapter isolates intersection behavior instead of assuming every constructed point automatically belongs to the model.

slides.title: Line-Circle Behavior Needs Witnesses
slides.notes: Separate the visual classification from the axiom's logical role. Secant, tangent, and outside cases are familiar, but the formal issue is when inside and outside witnesses force an actual point of intersection. This lets the class see why continuity-like assumptions enter construction arguments.

slides.title: The Extra Intersection Switch
slides.notes: This is a good moment to connect the formal axiom to compass-and-straightedge practice. Constructions often ask for a point where two circles meet, but a weak model may not contain that point. The E axiom adds the relevant existence behavior without collapsing all neutral geometry into Euclidean geometry by itself.

slides.title: Playfair's Axiom Is a Separate Choice
slides.notes: Avoid presenting Playfair as merely another technical clause. It changes the global parallel theory while leaving much of the neutral toolkit intact. The dashed alternatives in the visual are not claiming a specific hyperbolic model; they remind students that uniqueness is an additional decision, not a consequence of the earlier groups.

slides.title: Read Proofs as Dependency Paths
slides.notes: Treat this graph as a reading strategy for the whole chapter. When a proof invokes a construction or comparison, ask which earlier permission is being spent. This also prepares students for later chapters, where changing the model changes which dependency paths remain available.

slides.title: A Model-Auditing Protocol
slides.notes: End the body of the lecture by turning the chapter into a usable protocol. The point is not to certify an infinite model by sampling, but to learn the type of witness each axiom group demands. This keeps formal axioms connected to concrete mathematical behavior without pretending that pictures are proofs.

slides.title: What Hilbert Adds to Euclid
slides.notes: Close by returning to the initial motivation: Hilbert makes Euclidean reasoning inspectable. The students should now be able to describe a proof step by naming its permission, and they should be suspicious of models that look familiar but fail one switch. This sets up later chapters where coordinate fields and alternative geometries deliberately modify the underlying axiom bundle.
